title: MCP installation and diagnostic repair
description: An edited historical installation followed by its diagnostic debugging epilogue.

scenes.title: A cluster install, then a diagnostic fix
lines: EDITED REENACTMENT | IBM Storage Scale 6.0.1.1
Seven nodes | NFS, SMB and S3
Based on recorded calls and results from one session.
Some operator requests are reconstructed, not quotations.
Long-running operations are summarized.
Historical bugs are labeled; this is not a current runbook.
scenes.narration: This is an edited account of one cluster installation and the debugging session that followed it. The calls and results come from the project’s capture record. Some operator requests are reconstructed.

scenes.title: 1. Check the installer
lines: READ-ONLY CHECKS
Backend reachable; no installation already running.
Toolkit: IBM Storage Scale 6.0.1.1
Ansible and locale checked.
No cluster configured yet.
scenes.narration: We start by checking the installer. The backend is reachable, the toolkit is present, and no other operation is running. The agent checks Ansible, locale, and the existing configuration.

scenes.title: 2. Inspect nodes and disks
lines: HISTORICAL DIAGNOSTIC BUG
test_connection reports SSH failure.
list_devices reaches the same nodes.
Two storage servers: three unused 100 GB disks each.
Other nodes: operating-system disks only.
The diagnostic discrepancy is investigated after installation.
scenes.narration: Next, the agent inspects the machines and their disks. Each storage server has three unused hundred-gigabyte disks. A connection-test tool reports an error, but disk discovery reaches the same nodes successfully. The installation proceeds using that working path; the misleading diagnostic is investigated afterward.

scenes.title: 3. Read the environment details
lines: CAPTURED ENVIRONMENT DETAILS
Protocol interface: eth1
Separate from the protocol nodes’ own addresses.
S3 installation media reported present by the operator.
Windows client excluded from the seven-node cluster.
scenes.narration: The operator supplies the hosts file and confirms that S3 media is present. The agent identifies the reserved protocol addresses and their network interface, separate from the nodes’ own addresses.

scenes.title: 4. Start the toolkit service
lines: REQUEST SUMMARY — reconstructed wording
Set up the toolkit on the bastion installer.
start_setup(dry_run=true)
Inputs validated; nothing executed.
start_setup(dry_run=false)
SUCCESS; package distribution uses port 10080.
scenes.narration: The toolkit setup begins with a dry run, so the operator can review the intended action before execution. The agent then starts the setup service on the bastion installer. The recorded result is successful, with the package distribution service ready for the remaining configuration.

scenes.title: 5. Assign the seven node roles
lines: REQUEST SUMMARY — reconstructed wording
Two storage nodes: NSD, quorum, manager
One GUI node: GUI, quorum, admin
Two protocol nodes: protocol, manager
Two clients: client-only
Dry run reviewed; configuration lists all seven nodes.
scenes.narration: Now the seven nodes receive their roles. The two storage servers also provide quorum and management. The GUI node provides administration and quorum, while two protocol nodes serve clients. The agent reviews the dry run and confirms that all seven nodes appear in the configuration.

scenes.title: 6. Define the storage
lines: SIX NSDs, TWO FILESYSTEM NAMES
One disk per server -> cesSharedRoot
Two disks per server -> fs1
Separate failure groups for the two servers.
Placement is shown here; replica settings are not.
Verify replication separately before claiming redundancy.
scenes.narration: The storage request becomes six NSD definitions. One disk on each server is assigned to the protocol shared root, and the other disks to the main filesystem. Separate failure groups describe placement. Verify replication separately before claiming mirroring.

scenes.title: 7. Recover from configuration errors
lines: HISTORICAL ERRORS — not current call examples
Profile spelling rejected by the toolkit.
Unsupported performance-monitoring node flag rejected.
Retry omits both arguments -> SUCCESS
Callhome disabled; monitoring enabled; port range set.
Current MCP interface no longer accepts perfmon_node.
scenes.narration: Two configuration mistakes are left visible in this account. The toolkit rejects a profile spelling and an unsupported monitoring argument. The agent reads those errors, removes the arguments, and retries successfully. The unsupported parameter has since been removed from the MCP interface; this is historical recovery, not current usage.

scenes.title: 8. Configure the protocols
lines: GUI-BACKEND INTERACTION — summarized, not click footage
1. Configure CES shared root, mountpoint, interface and IPs.
2. Enable NFS, SMB and S3.
Both requests succeed.
The cluster definition lists all three protocols enabled.
scenes.narration: Protocol configuration uses the web interface’s backend. One request sets the shared root, mountpoint, interface, and floating addresses. A second enables NFS, SMB, and S3. Both succeed. We’re showing a summary of those requests here; the separate GUI tour shows the interface itself.

scenes.title: 9. Install and verify
lines: PRECHECK -> INSTALL -> POSTCHECK
Install precheck passed with recorded warnings.
Install completed in 26 minutes 18 seconds.
Postcheck: GPFS, NSDs, monitoring and GUI ACTIVE.
Deploy precheck: NFS, SMB and S3 checks passed.
scenes.narration: The installation precheck passes, and the installation takes about twenty-six minutes in the recorded run. The agent examines the log and completion status. A separate postcheck confirms GPFS, storage, monitoring, and the GUI. The protocol precheck then passes before deployment begins.

scenes.title: 10. Deploy and check the outcome
lines: DEPLOY RESULT — 17 minutes 31 seconds
An ASYNC FAILED line appears in the log.
Its task context and final results are checked.
Recap: failed=0, unreachable=0 on all seven nodes.
Filesystem, CES, S3, SMB, NFS, monitoring and GUI ACTIVE.
scenes.narration: Deployment takes about seventeen and a half minutes. One log line says async failed, so the agent checks its context rather than judging the whole run from that line. The final recap reports no failed or unreachable nodes, and the service checks confirm the intended components are active.

scenes.title: 11. Confirm, then investigate
lines: POSTCHECK-DEPLOY
Filesystem, CES, S3, SMB and NFS ACTIVE.
Performance monitoring and GUI ACTIVE.
SUCCESS — all services running.
NEXT CHAPTER: investigate the earlier connection-test error.
The cluster is already installed at this point.
scenes.narration: A final postcheck independently confirms the deployment. All services are running. Only now do we turn to the earlier connection-test problem. Keeping this order matters: the debugging evidence that follows comes from an installed, active cluster, not from the empty machines at the beginning.

scenes.title: 12. Reproduce the misleading error
lines: HISTORICAL BUG — later fixed
test_connection -> SSH failed, exit 255
list_devices -> reaches the same nodes
The cluster is active.
Compare the two tools before changing the environment.
scenes.narration: The operator asks for the connection test to be fixed. The agent reproduces the error and compares it with the tool that already works. Because the cluster is now active, the investigation can separate a real access problem from an inaccurate diagnosis by the tool.

scenes.title: 13. Compare the tools
lines: CODE REVIEW SUMMARY
Working tool: SSH uses configured user and port.
Old connection test: forces root and port 22.
Old test also calls every remote-command failure an SSH error.
Two hypotheses: overridden SSH settings and misclassified errors.
scenes.narration: Reading the code reveals two differences. The working tool lets SSH choose its configured user and port. The old connection test overrides both. It also treats any failure of the remote GPFS command as an SSH failure.

scenes.title: 14. Check the operator’s evidence
lines: OPERATOR-SUPPLIED RESULT
Manual check reaches the node on port 2223.
The GPFS table lists all seven nodes active.
Exit status: 0
The environment uses a different port from the old default.
scenes.narration: The operator supplies a successful manual check. Its output shows all seven nodes active, and the SSH message identifies port twenty-two twenty-three. That explains why forcing port twenty-two is wrong for this environment.

scenes.title: 15. Separate two kinds of failure
lines: READ-ONLY EXPERIMENTS
Correct port + working user -> SSH and GPFS checks pass.
Correct port + another user -> remote Permission denied.
Old tool mislabels the remote permission error as SSH failure.
Remote command failure is not the same as SSH failure.
scenes.narration: With the correct port, the check works. With a different user, the remote GPFS command reports permission denied, yet the old tool still calls it an SSH failure. That second experiment confirms the classification bug: reaching a host and successfully running a privileged command are different checks.

scenes.title: 16. Fix the diagnostic
lines: CODE CHANGE SUMMARY
User and port are optional; SSH configuration supplies defaults.
First test reachability with a harmless remote command.
Then check GPFS state separately.
Report remote-command failures accurately.
Regression checks added to backend and MCP layers.
scenes.narration: The fix makes user and port optional, allowing the installer’s SSH configuration to supply them. It checks reachability first and GPFS state second. A failing GPFS command can now be reported accurately without claiming SSH failed.

scenes.title: 17. Explain the incomplete redeploy
lines: BACKEND UPDATED; MCP CLIENT STILL HAS OLD DEFAULTS
New reachability check appears, but root:22 is still sent.
Explicit empty user/port -> configured SSH path works.
The remaining mismatch is in the loaded client tool definition.
scenes.narration: After the backend is redeployed, the new reachability step appears, but the request still carries the old user and port defaults. Explicitly clearing those values makes the check work. This narrows the remaining problem to the tool definition loaded by the MCP client, rather than the updated backend.

scenes.title: 18. Restart and confirm
lines: AFTER MCP RESTART
test_connection(node="scale-server1")
SSH reachable using configured settings.
GPFS state: all seven nodes active.
No user or port override needed.
Installation succeeded; diagnostic behavior now matches reality.
scenes.narration: After the MCP server is restarted, a call with only the node name works. SSH uses the configured settings, and the GPFS check reports the active cluster. The installation and the diagnostic repair are now both verified, with the client and backend using the same behavior.

scenes.title: Closing
lines: TWO OUTCOMES, VERIFIED SEPARATELY
A working NFS, SMB and S3 deployment.
A repaired connection-test tool.
Edited historical account; see the capture log for provenance.
Use the GUI tour or current runbook for the interface and setup.
scenes.narration: The useful lesson is to verify outcomes at each boundary: installation, deployment, remote access, and tool behavior. This recording keeps the successful checks and the mistakes that explain the repair. The capture log preserves the provenance, while the current runbook remains the reference for a new installation.
